title: Tear Fluid Proteomics: A Comparative Study of DIA and DDA Mass Spectrometry
projectDescription: Background: Mass spectrometry is a powerful technique for tear fluid proteomics, offering critical insights into its complex molecular composition. Data-dependent acquisition (DDA), the most commonly used approach, preferentially selects high-abundance proteins, limiting reproducibility and the quantification of low-abundance proteins. In contrast, data-independent acquisition (DIA) provides an unbiased and comprehensive proteomic profile by fragmenting all precursor ions, enhancing protein coverage, quantification accuracy and reproducibility. This study presents a comparative analysis of DDA and DIA approaches for tear fluid proteomics to improve detection of low-abundance proteins and facilitate biomarker discovery. Methods: Tear fluid samples were collected from healthy individuals using Schirmer strips, processed using in-strip protein digestion, and analyzed via liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS). DDA and DIA workflows were compared for proteomic depth, reproducibility, and data completeness. Quantification accuracy was assessed using serial dilutions of tear fluid samples in a complex biological matrix. Results: DIA identified 701 unique proteins and 2,444 peptides, significantly outperforming DDA, which identified 396 unique proteins and 1,447 peptides. DIA exhibited greater data completeness (78.7% proteins, 78.5% peptides) compared to DDA (42% proteins, 48% peptides) across replicates. Reproducibility was markedly improved in DIA, with median coefficients of variation (CVs) of 9.8% for proteins and 10.6% for peptides, compared to 17.3% and 22.3% in DDA, respectively. Quantification accuracy was also enhanced, demonstrating superior consistency across dilution series. Conclusion: This study demonstrates that DIA is a robust and reliable method for proteomic analysis of complex tear fluid samples, offering significantly greater depth, reproducibility, and accuracy compared to DDA.
sampleProcessingProtocol: The in-strip protein digestion method was used for protein extraction and digestion. Schirmer strips were lyophilized and cut into 5 × 2.5 mm pieces. Proteins were denatured using 120 µL of 8 M urea in 50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8), reduced with 10 mM dithiothreitol at 60 °C for 30 minutes, and alkylated with 55 mM iodoacetamide at room temperature for 30 minutes. The pH of each sample was adjusted to 8 using pH indicator strips (range 0–14; #13640516, Thermo Fisher Scientific). Mass spectrometry-grade trypsin (#90057, Thermo Fisher Scientific) was added at a 1:20 trypsin-to-protein (w/w) ratio, and digestion was carried out overnight at 37 °C. Following digestion, peptide concentrations were quantified using the Pierce Quantitative Colorimetric Peptide Assay (#23275, Thermo Fisher Scientific), yielding final concentrations between 200–250 µg/mL. An aliquot containing 125 µg of protein from each sample was purified using C18 spin columns, followed by lyophilization. Purified peptides were reconstituted in 80 µL of equilibration buffer (2% acetonitrile, 0.1% formic acid). To ensure a fair comparison between methods and eliminate sample-to-sample variability, a single pooled sample was prepared for LC-MS/MS analysis by combining 20 µL from each of the 15 purified samples. The final concentration of the pooled peptide sample was standardized to 0.2 µg/µL for consistent analysis.  LC-MS/MS analysis was performed using an Orbitrap Fusion Tribrid mass spectrometer coupled with an Ultimate 3000 nano-UPLC system (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA). Both DDA and DIA methods were evaluated for protein identification, reproducibility, and data completeness. For analysis, 5 µL (~1 µg) of pooled, reconstituted peptides were loaded onto a PepMap100 C18 trap column (5 µm, 0.3 × 5.0 mm, Thermo Fisher Scientific) and washed at a flow rate of 20 µL/min. Peptide separation was performed using a PepMap100 RSLC C18 analytical column (2.0 µm, 75 µm × 150 mm, Thermo Fisher Scientific) with a multistep gradient ranging from 2% to 40% acetonitrile in 0.1% formic acid. The gradient was applied over 100 minutes. The column was maintained at 40 °C with a flow rate of 300 nL/min. Mobile phase A consisted of 0.1% formic acid in water, while mobile phase B contained 0.1% formic acid in acetonitrile. LC-MS/MS was conducted in positive ion mode using a nano-electrospray ionization source, with a spray voltage of 2000 V and an ion transfer tube temperature of 300 °C.  The precursor mass scan was performed at a resolution of 60,000, with a maximum injection time of 58 ms and a standard AGC target mode, covering the m/z range of 400-1200. This was followed by 40 MS2 scans spanning the range of 300-1500 m/z. Precursor ion fragmentation was performed using higher-energy collisional dissociation (HCD) at a normalized collision energy of 30%. The isolation window was set to 20 m/z, and the total cycle time was 3 seconds.
dataProcessingProtocol: Raw DIA MS data were processed using DIA-NN (version 1.9) with default parameters. An in-silico DIA-NN–predicted spectral library was generated from the human UniProtKB/Swiss-Prot 2024 database (20,412 entries). For mixed samples, a combined spectral library was created using the respective human and E. coli UniProtKB/Swiss-Prot protein databases. DIA-NN parameters included Trypsin/P as the protease, allowance for one missed cleavage, N-terminal methionine excision, carbamidomethylation of cysteine, gene-level protein inference, and the Quant UMS (high precision) quantification approach. Additionally, the options "No shared spectra," "Heuristic protein inference," and "MBR" were enabled.
